title: Crack Initiation at Adhesive Layer Defects
introduction: In flexible photovoltaic module bonded joints, the adhesive layer may contain voids or defect-like regions introduced during manufacturing — particularly when excessive adhesive thickness leads to trapped air at the interface, or when bonding-area defects are present. Under mechanical loading, stress concentrates at these defect sites more readily than in a defect-free joint. This stress concentration reduces the effective fracture stress at the defect boundary, making crack initiation preferential at defect-adjacent interfaces and shifting the failure mode from cohesive fracture within the adhesive to adhesive failure along the interface.
reasoning: The 337-Elsevier adhesive joint study shows that both voids from excessive thickness and introduced bonding defects create stress concentration sites that initiate interfacial cracks under mechanical loading, reducing joint tensile-shear strength.

key_findings.claim: Defects in the adhesive layer create stress concentration sites under mechanical loading, promoting crack initiation
key_findings.detail: In adhesive joints where the adhesive layer contains voids or defect-like regions, stress concentration occurs more easily at defect sites during loading. [^elsevier337a] Additionally, residual stress from curing shrinkage increases with adhesive thickness, further contributing to stress concentration at defect boundaries. [^elsevier337b]

key_findings.claim: Adhesive failure and interfacial crack initiation occur preferentially around bonding defects under mechanical load
key_findings.detail: When the adhesive joint contains bonding-area defects, adhesive failure occurs more readily around those defects during loading. [^elsevier337c] Cracks initiate along the interface between the adhesive and the adherend in the region surrounding the defect, producing a mixed failure mode combining adhesive and cohesive fracture.
